decision.explanation: Write v=x+iy with x=(0,2)^T and y=(-1,3)^T. Equating real and imaginary parts gives Ax=x−6y and Ay=6x+y. Thus P=[x,−y] satisfies AP=PC, and det(P)=−2≠0, so A=PCP⁻¹. This directly gives option b. The matrix is not unique; option d also satisfies the relation.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ 6 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1+6\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ -6 & 1\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ 6 & 1\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=1-6\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that for any 2×2 real matrix A with complex eigenvalues, we have A=PCP−1, where

P=[||Re(v)Im(v)||],C=[Re(λ)Im(λ)−Im(λ)Re(λ)],

and v is an eigenvector of A corresponding to the complex eigenvalue λ.

First, notice that

[Re(λ)Im(λ)−Im(λ)Re(λ)]=[16−61]≠C,

while

[Re(λ―)Im(λ―)−Im(λ―)Re(λ―)]=[1−661]=C.

So, our rotation-scaling matrix C corresponds to the eigenvalue λ―=1−6i, the complex conjugate of λ. Hence, to construct the matrix P, we use the eigenvector v―, the complex conjugate of v.

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

v―=[i2−3i]=[02]⏟Re(v―)+i[1−3]⏟Im(v―)

Finally, we can now construct P:

P=[||Re(v―)Im(v―)||]=[012−3].

content.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Using the Complex Conjugate
content.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ 6 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1+6\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ -6 & 1\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ 6 & 1\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=1-6\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is λ²−8λ+52, so the eigenvalues are 4±6i. Since C is a rotation-scaling matrix, (a+ib,c+id)ᵀ is an eigenvector for one of these eigenvalues. after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & -3 \\ 15 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +52 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=4\pm 6\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =4-6\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=4-6\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4-6\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4-6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3+6\text{i} & -3 \\ 15 & -3+6\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(3+6\text{i}){x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 15{x}_{1}+(-3+6\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(1+2\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1+2\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=\frac{1}{5}.

content.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Given Only One Eigenvalue
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & -3 \\ 15 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +52 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=4\pm 6\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =4-6\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=4-6\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4-6\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4-6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3+6\text{i} & -3 \\ 15 & -3+6\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(3+6\text{i}){x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 15{x}_{1}+(-3+6\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(1+2\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1+2\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(v)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(v)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i}-1 \\ \text{i}+2\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2+3\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=2-3\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}-1-2\text{i} \\ 2-\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Using the Complex Conjugate
content.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i}-1 \\ \text{i}+2\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2+3\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=2-3\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}-1-2\text{i} \\ 2-\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is λ²+2λ+5, giving eigenvalues −1±2i. Since C is a rotation-scaling matrix, z=(a+ib,c+id)ᵀ is an eigenvector for one of these eigenvalues.
